claims.claim: pm2-logrotate compression has never worked: 0 of the rotated files in ~/.pm2/logs are .gz, because the installed module parses compress with a string-only parseBool while PM2 passes boolean true.
claims.evidence:
All checks were read-only on oracle-cto-aipa, 2026-10-09 10:23 UTC.

1) No rotated file is compressed (CONFIRMED)
- In ~/.pm2/logs there are 107 files matching `__YYYY-...log` and 0 matching `__*.gz`.
- I read the first 2 bytes of all 107 rotated files: none has the gzip header 1f8b, so none is compressed under a .log name either.
- The 5 .gz files in that folder were compressed by hand, not by the module: the four dragontrade-binance/bybit-*.log.gz files are dated May 25, and dragontrade-main-out.2026-01-16_to_2026-09-28.log.gz is dated Sep 28 15:31, 6 minutes before the module was installed. None has the `__` rotation name.
- I searched every pm2-logrotate-out*.log for ".gz": 0 hits in 125 "has been created" lines.

2) It has never worked (CONFIRMED since the 28 Sep install)
- pm2 jlist shows the pm2-logrotate process (pid 234579) has run without a break since 2026-09-28T15:37:05Z.
- COMPRESSION is computed once, when the module loads (app.js:49).
- Its first rotation, ~/.pm2/pm2__2026-09-28_15-38-05.log (882455872 bytes), was written uncompressed.
- The oldest surviving rotated files are dated 2026-09-29_00-00-00, all .log.

3) Root cause (CONFIRMED in effect)
- The installed module is 3.0.0. In app.js, lines 38-42 are `const parseBool = (str, defaultVal = false) => { if (str === 'true') return true; if (str === 'false') return false; return defaultVal; }` and line 49 is `var COMPRESSION = parseBool(conf.compress, false);`.
- I ran a read-only node simulation on the box using the module's own pmx 1.6.8 Autocast: `raw compress: "true" string` -> `after Autocast: true boolean` -> `parseBool(compress): false`.

4) "PM2 passes boolean true" is WRONG: PM2 passes the string "true"
- ~/.pm2/module_conf.json holds `"compress": "true"`, a string.
- The running process's environment (/proc/234579/environ) holds `pm2-logrotate={...,"compress":"true",...}`, also a string.
- pm2 jlist shows the same, with typeof string.
- The string becomes a boolean only inside the module, in its pmx dependency: ~/.pm2/modules/pm2-logrotate/node_modules/pmx/lib/configuration.js:97, `var casted_conf = Autocast(JSON.parse(process.env[conf.module_name]))`. Autocast's common_strings maps 'true' to true.
- So the module breaks itself: its own config library converts the value before its own parseBool reads it.
- The round-1 report says this two ways. Line 20 ("PM2's config loader passes the boolean true") repeats the error. Line 331 ("pmx Autocast turns the config string 'true' into the boolean true") is correct.
claims.correction:
pm2-logrotate compression has never worked since the module started on 28 Sep 15:37 UTC. All 107 rotated *__*.log files in ~/.pm2/logs are uncompressed: 0 are .gz and 0 have the gzip header. The 5 .gz files in the folder were compressed by hand earlier. The 842 MB pm2 daemon log it rotated at 15:38:05 was also left uncompressed.

Cause: pm2-logrotate 3.0.0 reads compress through a parseBool that only accepts the string 'true' (app.js:38-49). PM2 itself passes the string "true": module_conf.json and the process environment both hold "compress":"true". But the module's own pmx 1.6.8 dependency converts that string to the boolean true (configuration.js:97, Autocast) before parseBool sees it. parseBool does not recognise a boolean, so it returns the default, false.

claims.claim: The 28 Sep pm2-logrotate install left ~/.pm2/pm2__2026-09-28_15-38-05.log (~842 MB) uncompressed, and nothing will ever rotate or remove it.
claims.evidence:
The first half of the claim holds up. The second half ("nothing will EVER rotate or remove it") is too strong. pm2-logrotate's own retain=10 rule does cover this file, but the condition that triggers it is extremely unlikely at the current log rate.

1) The file exists, is about 842 MiB, is uncompressed, and was made by pm2-logrotate:
`ssh oracle-cto-aipa 'ls -la ~/.pm2/'` gives
`-rw-rw-r-- 1 ubuntu ubuntu 882455872 Sep 28 15:38 pm2__2026-09-28_15-38-05.log` (882,455,872 B = 841.6 MiB)
`-rw-rw-r-- 1 ubuntu ubuntu     51960 Oct  9 06:48 pm2.log`
- The old file runs from `2026-01-07T19:54:19: PM2 log: --- New PM2 Daemon started` to `2026-09-28T15:37:05: PM2 log: App [pm2-logrotate:10] online`.
- The current pm2.log starts at `2026-09-28T16:07:28`.
- The `__YYYY-MM-DD_HH-mm-ss` name comes from app.js:113 (`file.substr(0, file.length - 4) + '__' + final_time + '.log'`). The time is 60 s after the module came online (workerInterval "60"), so the module's first worker tick produced it. The `pm2 install` itself did not.
- Why it is uncompressed:
  - `module_conf.json` has `"compress": "true"`.
  - pmx `configuration.js:97` runs `Autocast(JSON.parse(...))`, and autocast.js maps `'true': true`.
  - app.js:38-42 `parseBool` only accepts the string `'true'`, so `COMPRESSION = false`.
  - Corroborated: `ls ~/.pm2/logs | grep "__2026"` gives 107 files, of which 0 are `.gz`.

2) "Nothing will ever rotate or remove it" is too strong:
- Rotation is only by size: app.js:224 `proceed_file(PM2_ROOT_PATH + '/pm2.log', false)`. The midnight cron (app.js:229-248) force-rotates only `proceed_app(app, true)`, never pm2.log. The size check (line 172) is `data.size >= SIZE_LIMIT || force`, with SIZE_LIMIT = 50M.
- But after every pm2.log rotation, `delete_old(file)` (lines 69-93) uses `fileBaseName = 'pm2__'` in `~/.pm2` and unlinks anything past `RETAIN` (10). `pm2__2026-09-28_15-38-05.log` matches, so it is in scope. It gets deleted on the 10th future rotation of pm2.log, which needs 10 x 50 MiB = about 524 MB of new daemon log.
- At today's rate (51,960 B over about 10.8 days, roughly 4.8 KB/day) that would take centuries, so in practice never.
- At the old file's own Jan 7 to Sep 28 average (882 MB / 264 days, roughly 3.3 MB/day) it would take about 5 months.
- A PM2 restart loop like the earlier dragontrade one writes several lines per restart and could bring that much sooner. So "never" is a projection based on current traffic, not a structural fact.

3) No other mechanism touches the file (checked, so the claim is right on this point):
- `crontab -l` has no `rm`/`find -delete`/`flush`/`.pm2` cleanup. A grep of check_oracle_health.sh, health_monitor.sh, oci_keepalive.sh, hs-watch-manual-emails.sh and github-token-watch.sh only hits `pm2 jlist`.
- Root has no crontab ("no crontab for root").
- `ls /etc/logrotate.d` has no pm2 entry, and `grep -rl pm2 /etc/logrotate.d /etc/logrotate.conf /etc/cron*` finds nothing.
- The systemd timers (system and user) are all stock or espaluz-json-guard (a Postgres snapshot).
- tmpfiles.d has nothing for /home/ubuntu/.pm2.
- A file that has already been rotated is never itself rotated or compressed again by pm2-logrotate.

Everything above was read-only: ls, head/tail -c, cat, grep, crontab -l, systemctl list-timers/cat. Nothing was changed.
claims.correction: pm2-logrotate's first worker tick, at 15:38:05 on 28 Sep (60 s after the module came online), copied the 842 MiB PM2 daemon log (7 Jan to 28 Sep) to ~/.pm2/pm2__2026-09-28_15-38-05.log (882,455,872 B) and did not compress it, because compress="true" is broken by the pmx Autocast/parseBool mismatch. Nothing outside pm2-logrotate (cron, /etc/logrotate.d, systemd timers, tmpfiles) will ever touch it, and it will never be compressed after the fact. It is not completely out of scope, though. pm2-logrotate's retain=10 rule matches the 'pm2__' prefix and would delete it on the 10th future size-based rotation of pm2.log, which needs about 524 MB more daemon log. pm2.log grows about 4.8 KB/day today (52 KB since 28 Sep), so in practice that will not happen without manual action. At the old 3.3 MB/day average, or during a PM2 restart loop, it could happen within months.

claims.claim: health_monitor.sh runs every 5 minutes from cron and has logged "WARNING: High disk usage" many times, but it only writes to ~/health.log and sends no alert (no Telegram, no email) to anyone.
claims.evidence:
I tried to refute the claim and could not. Every part of it holds on the live box. All commands were read-only, over ssh oracle-cto-aipa.

1. It runs every 5 minutes from cron.
   - `crontab -l` line 4: `*/5 * * * * /home/ubuntu/health_monitor.sh`
   - `systemctl is-active cron` returns `active`.
   - `journalctl -u cron --since "2026-10-09 09:50"` shows a run every 5 minutes, for example `Oct 09 09:50:01 ... CRON[3869613]: (ubuntu) CMD (/home/ubuntu/health_monitor.sh)`, then 09:55, 10:00, 10:05, 10:10, 10:15 and 10:20. So it actually fires, not just sits in the crontab.

2. It has logged the disk warning many times.
   - `wc -l ~/health.log` gives 1000 lines.
   - `grep -c "WARNING: High disk usage" ~/health.log` gives 500.
   - The oldest line kept is `2026-10-07 16:45:01 | WARNING: High disk usage: 95%`. The newest is `2026-10-09 10:20:01 | WARNING: High disk usage: 98%`.

3. It only writes to ~/health.log and alerts nobody.
   - `cat /home/ubuntu/health_monitor.sh` (814 bytes, dated Jan 24 2026) sets `LOG_FILE=/home/ubuntu/health.log`. Every `echo` in it ends in `>> $LOG_FILE`. Its last action is `tail -1000 $LOG_FILE > $LOG_FILE.tmp && mv ...`.
   - It contains no curl, no Telegram call, no mail and no webhook.
   - It prints nothing to stdout, so cron has nothing to send either.
   - The live copy is identical to the repo file `docs/oracle/health_monitor.sh` (`diff` printed nothing).

4. I also looked for any other path that could carry an alert. None exists.
   - The crontab has no `MAILTO` line (`grep -i mailto` returned exit code 1).
   - No mail program is installed: `which mail sendmail msmtp` printed nothing and failed.
   - `/var/mail` is empty.
   - Nothing else reads ~/health.log. `check_oracle_health.sh` only matched because it writes `LOG=/var/log/oracle-health.log`, which is a different file. Grepping Oracle's `~/cto-aipa/dist`, `~/cto-aipa/scripts`, `~/bin` and `~/*.sh` finds only health_monitor.sh itself. In the local repos (cto-aipa `src` and `scripts`, VibeJobHunterAIPA_AIMCF `src` and `scripts`), the only reference is `docs/oracle/health_monitor.sh:4`.

One small caveat: "many times" can only be counted inside the window the log keeps. The script trims the file to its last 1000 lines (about 42 hours, back to 7 Oct 16:45), so any earlier warnings are already gone. That does not weaken the claim. It means the file deletes its own history, as round 1 already noted.

claims.claim: espaluz-webhook.service has been crash-looping (Address already in use on port 5000, held by espaluz-payments-webhook) since late June, the live health check restarts it every 5 minutes, and the StartLimitIntervalSec/StartLimitBurst brake is ignored because it sits in the [Service] section.
claims.evidence:
All checks were read-only, on oracle-cto-aipa at 2026-10-09 ~10:24-10:30 UTC, systemd 255 (255.4-1ubuntu8.17).

CONFIRMED: the crash loop on port 5000, held by the payments unit
- `systemctl status espaluz-webhook` -> "Active: activating (auto-restart) (Result: exit-code)", "code=exited, status=1/FAILURE".
- `journalctl -u espaluz-webhook` -> a cycle about every 10.25 s ("Scheduled restart job, restart counter is at 4435/4436/4437..."). The oldest journal entry (Sep 22 18:09:58) already shows "restart counter is at 90588".
- `sudo ss -ltnp | grep :5000` -> `0.0.0.0:5000 users:(("python",pid=1031872,fd=3))`. `systemctl show espaluz-payments-webhook -p MainPID` -> 1031872 (active since Oct 1 06:58:40).
- `tail /var/log/espaluz-webhook.log` -> "Address already in use / Port 5000 is in use by another program".

CONFIRMED: it started in late June
- `grep -m1 -b -n "Address already in use"` -> line 252723, offset 34414570. The line before it reads "2026-06-28 11:32:56,781 - INFO - Starting PayPal Webhook Server on port 5000...".
- `ls -la --time-style=full-iso` -> espaluz-payments-webhook.service was written 2026-06-28 11:32:46.
- Checking the whole log for "Running on" vs "Address already in use" gives one change only: a successful bind near the top (line 17), then EADDR from line 252723 to the end. The old unit never bound the port again.

CONFIRMED: the live health check restarts it every 5 minutes
- `crontab -l` -> "*/5 * * * * /home/ubuntu/check_oracle_health.sh".
- Script lines 62-66: "if ! systemctl is-active --quiet espaluz-webhook ... sudo systemctl restart espaluz-webhook".
- `journalctl` at 10:25:02 -> "sudo[3882997]: ubuntu : ... COMMAND=/usr/bin/systemctl restart espaluz-webhook", then "Stopped espaluz-webhook.service", "Started ...", "Main process exited ... status=1/FAILURE".
- 126 such sudo restarts today (00:00-10:25).
- awk over /var/log/oracle-health.log from the "=== 2026-06-28T11:35" header: runs=29651, restarts=29637. The first "espaluz-webhook not active" comes right after "=== 2026-06-28T11:35:01+00:00 ===".

PARTLY: why the brake fails
- `systemctl cat` -> the drop-in resilience.conf has "[Service] Restart=always RestartSec=10 StartLimitIntervalSec=300 StartLimitBurst=10". The main unit has no StartLimit keys, and DropInPaths lists only resilience.conf.
- The journal prints only "resilience.conf:4: Unknown key name 'StartLimitIntervalSec' in section 'Service', ignoring." There is no such warning for StartLimitBurst.
- `systemctl show` -> StartLimitIntervalUSec=10s and StartLimitBurst=10. /etc/systemd/system.conf has "#DefaultStartLimitBurst=5" (commented out, so the default is 5). The live value of 10 proves systemd accepted the StartLimitBurst key from [Service] as a legacy compatibility alias.
- So only the interval key is ignored. The interval falls back to the 10 s default, and 10 starts in 10 s can never happen with RestartSec=10, so the brake never trips.
claims.correction:
espaluz-webhook.service has crash-looped since 2026-06-28 11:32:56 with "Address already in use" on port 5000. Port 5000 is held by espaluz-payments-webhook (pid 1031872), whose unit file was installed at 11:32:46 the same minute. check_oracle_health.sh (cron */5) runs `sudo systemctl restart espaluz-webhook` on almost every run: 29,637 restarts in 29,651 runs since 2026-06-28 11:35, and 126 today by 10:25.

The brake is only half-ignored. systemd rejects StartLimitIntervalSec in [Service] ("Unknown key name ... ignoring"), so the interval stays at the 10 s default. StartLimitBurst=10 in [Service] IS applied as a legacy alias: `systemctl show` reports StartLimitBurst=10, not the default 5. The brake can never trip because 10 starts within 10 s is impossible with RestartSec=10. It does not fail because both keys are ignored.

Caveat: moving the keys to [Unit] would cut the loop to bursts but not stop it. Each 5-minute health-check restart would still be allowed once the 300 s window has passed.

claims.claim: Ubuntu's systemd-tmpfiles cleaner on this box deletes /tmp entries only after 30 days of no access, so scratch from 2-6 Oct stays; it is not 'only at boot'.
claims.evidence:
All checks were read-only, run on oracle-cto-aipa (Ubuntu 24.04.3 LTS, systemd 255.4-1ubuntu8.17).

What holds up:
1. `cat /usr/lib/tmpfiles.d/tmp.conf` shows `D /tmp 1777 root root 30d`. This is the stock file: its md5 `23cea5c227ac9238a1c8cc2acbe644eb` matches `/var/lib/dpkg/info/systemd.md5sums`. Nothing in /etc/tmpfiles.d overrides it (that folder only has screen-cleanup.conf).
2. `findmnt -T /tmp` shows /tmp is the root ext4 disk (`/dev/sda1 ext4 rw,relatime`), not tmpfs.
3. `systemctl cat systemd-tmpfiles-clean.timer` shows `OnBootSec=15min` and `OnUnitActiveSec=1d`. The service runs `systemd-tmpfiles --clean`. The journal shows it finished on Oct 08 03:19 and Oct 09 03:19 (`Result=success`). The next run is Sat 2026-10-10 03:19 UTC. So it really is a daily age-based cleaner, not "only at boot".
4. The man page (tmpfiles.d.5) says: "By default, any of these ... values will prevent cleanup if it is more recent than the current time minus the age field". The age-by field defaults to `abcmABM`.
5. Field proof that a recent access resets the clock: `stat /tmp/repro.py` gives M=2026-09-04 and A=2026-10-03, and the file is still present after the Oct 9 clean. `stat /tmp/tg-sync-20260630132219` gives M=2026-06-30 and A=2026-10-08 22:21, and it is also still present.
6. Scratch from 2–6 Oct: 366 top-level /tmp entries are dated 2026-10-02..06 and still present. Under the daily rule the earliest any of them can go is about 1–5 Nov.

What does not hold up exactly:
A. "Deletes /tmp entries ONLY after 30 days" is false when the box reboots. `systemctl cat systemd-tmpfiles-setup.service` shows `ExecStart=systemd-tmpfiles --create --remove --boot --exclude-prefix=/dev`. tmpfiles.d(5) line 198 says type `D` means "the contents of the directory will be removed when --remove is used". So every boot wipes all of /tmp, whatever its age. Exempt are /tmp/systemd-private-* (`x` in systemd-tmp.conf) and the snap-private-tmp internals (`X` in snapd's conf), but those are not scratch. The scratch from 2–6 Oct survives only because the box has not rebooted: `uptime -s` gives 2026-05-13 02:53:27.
B. "30 days of no access" is too narrow. The clock is the NEWEST of atime, mtime and birth time (btime), plus ctime for files only (not for directories). Modifying, creating or chmod-ing an entry also resets it, not just reading it.
C. Side observation: many old /tmp directories show the same atime, 2026-10-08 22:21:00–01 (tg-sync-*, atlas-deploy, _cj, tmux-1001, manual-cycle-*). That points to one sweep that read those folders, plausibly an earlier investigation pass, though I could not tie it to a specific command. Because directory atime (`A`) counts for directories, that sweep pushed back cleanup of those directories by about 30 days. The round-1 report already records the same effect for the 8 espaluz_video_*.mp4 files (line 469).
claims.correction: On this box /tmp is cleaned two ways. (1) systemd-tmpfiles-clean.timer runs daily at about 03:19 UTC and deletes entries whose newest of access, modify and birth time (plus status-change time for files) is more than 30 days old. (2) systemd-tmpfiles-setup.service wipes all of /tmp on every boot, because `D` together with `--remove --boot` empties the folder regardless of age. So it is not "only at boot", and it is not "only after 30 days" either. The scratch from 2–6 Oct stays until about 1–5 Nov at the earliest, or later if anything touches it, but only as long as the server does not reboot. It has been up since 13 May 2026. Any read or write of a file, and any listing of a directory, restarts its 30-day clock, including the investigators' own scans.

claims.claim: The repo copy of scripts/oracle-resilience/check_oracle_health.sh still contains the old dragontrade restart loop that the live Oracle copy fixed by hand on 25 May, so a redeploy from the repo would bring the loop back.
claims.evidence:
Everything was checked read-only on 9 Oct 2026. Nothing was changed on Oracle or in the repo.

1. The repo copy still has the loop. Local HEAD 3a04779 equals origin/main.
   - `cat -n scripts/oracle-resilience/check_oracle_health.sh`, lines 49-54: `for app in dragontrade-main dragontrade-dashboard dragontrade-bybit dragontrade-binance; do` / `if ! pm2 describe "$app" 2>/dev/null | grep -q "status: online"; then` ... `pm2 restart "$app"`.
   - `git log -- <file>` returns a single commit: 2993bba (2026-03-28).
   - `gh api .../contents/...?ref=main` shows the same lines 49-50 on GitHub main. It also shows `deploy_on_server.sh` lines 45-46 with the same loop.
   - Oracle's own checkout has the same loop: `/home/ubuntu/cto-aipa/scripts/oracle-resilience/check_oracle_health.sh:50` and `deploy_on_server.sh:46`.

2. The live copy was fixed by hand on 25 May.
   - `stat /home/ubuntu/check_oracle_health.sh` gives `2026-05-25 14:46:39 ... 2848`.
   - Lines 35-48 of the live file carry the comment `# May 25 2026 FIX: use jq on pm2 jlist. The previous grep "status: online" NEVER matched...`. The loop now covers only `for app in dragontrade-main dragontrade-dashboard` and reads `pm2 jlist | jq ... .pm2_env.status`.
   - A backup, `check_oracle_health.sh.pre-may25-fix` (May 25 14:33), sits next to it. `diff` between the two shows the old 4-app grep loop was replaced by the jq version.
   - Cron still runs the live file: `*/5 * * * * /home/ubuntu/check_oracle_health.sh`.

3. The old grep still never matches, so the loop would come back. pm2 is 6.0.14.
   - `pm2 describe dragontrade-main | grep status` returns `│ status            │ online │`, with no colon.

claims.evidence:
All checks were read-only, run over ssh oracle-cto-aipa on 9 Oct 2026. I also ran git grep in D:/aideazz/VibeJobHunterAIPA_AIMCF.

PARTS THAT HOLD
- `du -sh ~/VibeJobHunterAIPA_AIMCF/logs` returned `290M`. `ls logs | grep -c '^vibejobhunter_'` returned `100`, and there are no other files. The sizes add up to 303,082,593 bytes.
- Nothing rotates or deletes these files:
  - `/etc/logrotate.d` holds only alternatives, apport, apt, bootlog, btmp, certbot, cloud-init, dpkg, fail2ban, nginx, postgresql-common, rsyslog, ubuntu-pro-client, unattended-upgrades and wtmp. `grep -ril vibejob` over logrotate, /etc/cron*, tmpfiles.d found nothing.
  - The user crontab has no entry that removes or rotates `VibeJobHunterAIPA_AIMCF/logs`.
  - `git grep RotatingFileHandler|TimedRotatingFileHandler|logrotate` in the VJH repo found nothing.
  - `src/utils/logger.py:48-50` uses a plain `logging.FileHandler(log_file)`.

PARTS THAT ARE WRONG
1. "A new file every day" is false. The filename is set once, when the logger is created at process start (`datetime.now().strftime('%Y%m%d')`). So a new file appears only when a VJH process starts:
   - `systemctl show vibejobhunter` shows `ActiveEnterTimestamp=Wed 2026-10-07 21:14:43 UTC`, and `/proc/3353377/fd` points to `logs/vibejobhunter_20261007.log`, still being written on 9 Oct (`mtime 2026-10-09 10:09`).
   - vibejobhunter-web (pid 1031933, started 1 Oct) still writes `vibejobhunter_20261001.log`.
   - The 100 files span 18 Jan to 7 Oct, about 263 days. In October there are only 20261001, 1005, 1006 and 1007; there are no files for 2, 3, 4, 8 or 9 Oct.
2. "DEBUG-level" is false in practice. The file handler is set to DEBUG, but `logger.py:25` sets the logger itself to `logger.setLevel(logging.INFO)`, which drops DEBUG records before they reach the handler. Level counts across all 100 files: `828808 | INFO`, `9416 | WARNING`, `403 | ERROR`, and zero DEBUG records. The only two files containing the word "DEBUG" (20260406 and 20260407) are INFO lines with `DELIVERY_DEBUG: email_sent=...` in the message text.
3. The size is not spread across daily files, and it is not current growth:
   - One file, `vibejobhunter_20260516.log`, is 221,397,847 bytes, 73% of the folder. It was last modified `2026-06-21 18:26`. It has 3,087,187 lines, but only 61,887 are INFO records. The bulk is 88,811 repeated Telegram tracebacks: `88811 Exception happened while polling for updates.` with `telegram/ext/_updater.py` stack frames.
   - The next biggest files are 8.4, 8.0, 8.0 and 6.4 MB, from January and May.
   - Since the 28 Sep cleanup the folder grew by only 3,067,450 bytes, across 9 files modified after `2026-09-28 15:45`. So the round-1 figure of "+473 MB under ~/VibeJobHunter* since 28 Sep" did not come from logs/.
claims.correction:
VibeJobHunter's logger (`src/utils/logger.py`, a plain FileHandler with no rotation) starts a new `vibejobhunter_YYYYMMDD.log` each time a VJH process starts, not each day. The date in the name is the start date, and a long-running process keeps writing to the same file: the current one started 7 Oct is still being written on 9 Oct. That gives 100 files over about 263 days, totalling 290 MB, and nothing rotates or deletes them (no logrotate rule, no cron job, no cleanup code).

The handler is set to DEBUG, but the logger itself is set to INFO, so the files contain only INFO, WARNING and ERROR records and no DEBUG records at all.

73% of the 290 MB (221 MB) is a single file, `vibejobhunter_20260516.log`. Nothing has written to it since 21 Jun, and its bulk is 88,811 repeated Telegram "Exception happened while polling for updates" tracebacks. Since 28 Sep the folder has grown only about 3 MB, so it was not a meaningful cause of the October disk fill. Fixing this means dealing with that one dormant file and adding rotation; changing the log level would not help.
